content: Inducible T-cell costimulator (ICOS), also known as CD278, is a protein encoded by the ICOS gene in humans. It is a member of the CD28 superfamily of costimulatory molecules and is expressed on activated T cells. ICOS is particularly significant for the function of Th2 cells. The ICOS protein belongs to the CD28 and CTLA-4 family of cell-surface receptors. It forms homodimers and plays a critical role in cell-to-cell signaling, immune response modulation, and the regulation of cell proliferation. In studies involving ICOS-deficient (ICOS-/-) T cells, these cells exhibited reduced proliferation and decreased secretion of interleukin-2 (IL-2) when activated with plate-bound anti-CD3 antibodies, compared to wild-type naïve T cells. However, the addition of IL-2 to the culture restored the proliferative capacity of ICOS-/T cells. This suggests that the defect in proliferation is likely due to ICOS-mediated IL-2 secretion or the activation of signaling pathways shared by ICOS and IL-2. Regarding cytokine secretion, ICOS-/CD4+ T cells activated in vitro showed reduced secretion of IL-4, a Th2-associated cytokine, while maintaining normal levels of IFN-γ, a Th1-associated cytokine. Similarly, CD4+ T cells isolated from ICOS-/mice immunized with keyhole limpet hemocyanin (KLH) in alum or complete Freund's adjuvant exhibited diminished IL-4 secretion upon recall with KLH, but their IFN-γ and IL-5 secretion remained comparable to that of wild-type cells. These findings align with observations in an airway hypersensitivity model, where ICOS-/mice sensitized with ovalbumin (Ova) protein showed reduced IL-4 secretion but normal IL-5 secretion. This indicates a specific defect in Th2 cytokine secretion, without impairing Th1 differentiation, as both IL-4 and IL-5 are associated with Th2 responses. Consistent with the reduced Th2 responses, ICOS-/mice demonstrated impaired germinal center formation and lower titers of IgG1 and IgE antibodies following immunization. In the context of combination therapy, patients treated with ipilimumab, an anti-CTLA-4 antibody, exhibited increased levels of ICOS+ T cells in both tumor tissues and peripheral blood. This increase served as a pharmacodynamic biomarker for anti-CTLA-4 therapy. In wild-type C57BL/6 mice, anti-CTLA-4 treatment led to tumor rejection in 80–90% of cases. However, in mice deficient in either ICOS or its ligand (ICOSLG), the efficacy of anti-CTLA-4 therapy dropped to less than 50%. When an agonistic stimulus targeting the ICOS pathway was combined with anti-CTLA-4 therapy, the treatment efficacy increased by approximately four to five times compared to control treatments. As of 2015, antibodies targeting ICOS were not yet available for clinical testing.
